findings.title: Untrusted project settings can run arbitrary external formatters (including live guest edits)
findings.description: Zed 0.154.0 applies `.zed/settings.json` from the opened worktree with no worktree-trust gate. Language settings are resolved with the buffer's worktree location, so a project can set `formatter.external.command` / `arguments`. Default `format_on_save` is `on`. On save (or explicit format), `format_via_external_command` spawns that command with the user's privileges. A ReadWrite collaborator can edit `.zed/settings.json` on the host; `SettingsObserver` reloads it live, so the next host save formats via the attacker-chosen binary. This tree predates the later worktree-trust fix (GHSA-29cp-2hmh-hcxj / CVE-2025-68432 class).
findings.impact: Opening a malicious repository, or inviting a malicious collaborator with edit access, yields host arbitrary code execution as the Zed user without installing an extension.
findings.attack_path:
1. Attacker ships `.zed/settings.json` with languages/defaults `formatter: { external: { command: "/tmp/pwn", arguments: [] } }` (format_on_save remains on), or a ReadWrite guest writes that file into a shared project.
2. Host opens the project (or already has it open); SettingsObserver loads/reloads local settings.
3. Host saves any buffer whose language inherits that formatter.
4. `Project::format_via_external_command` runs `Command::new(command)` with attacker args.
findings.remediation: Do not apply project language/formatter settings until the worktree is explicitly trusted. Block `formatter.external` (and similar exec sinks) in Restricted Mode. Treat collaborator edits to `.zed/settings.json` as trust-boundary changes requiring re-confirmation. Prefer allowlisting formatter binaries.
findings.poc_video_notes: A PoC video was not produced: headless scan with no Slack/video destination. Exploitability validated by tracing settings load → language_settings(file) → FormatOnSave::On → Formatter::External → smol::process::Command::new(command).

findings.title: Project lsp.binary.path via extensions spawns attacker-chosen host processes
findings.description: Bundled and third-party extensions resolve LSP commands with `LspSettings::for_worktree`, which reads worktree-local ProjectSettings (including `.zed/settings.json`). Extensions such as zig, ruby (solargraph/ruby-lsp/rubocop), ruff, csharp, and lexical honor `binary.path` / `binary.arguments` and return them as the language server Command. `ExtensionLspAdapter` then starts that path via the normal LSP spawn path. Built-in adapters in this commit often call `ProjectSettings::get_global` (so they miss project lsp.binary), but any installed extension that uses `for_worktree` restores the RCE sink. Guests with edit access can change project LSP settings while the host has the project open; LSP restart logic picks up the new binary.
findings.impact: Malicious repo or collaborator-controlled `.zed/settings.json` executes arbitrary binaries when the matching language file is opened or the language server restarts—host RCE as the Zed user.
findings.attack_path:
1. Attacker places `.zed/settings.json` with e.g. `lsp.zls.binary.path` pointing at a payload in-repo (or absolute path), or a guest edits that file on a shared project.
2. Host has the zig (or ruby/ruff/csharp/…) extension enabled and opens a matching source file.
3. Extension `language_server_command` returns the configured path/args.
4. Host spawns the language server process → payload runs.
findings.remediation: Gate project `lsp.*.binary` on worktree trust. Ignore or prompt before spawning binaries that are not under the extension work dir or a user-approved allowlist. Restarting language servers after collaborator settings edits should require host confirmation.
findings.poc_video_notes: A PoC video was not produced. Chain validated by reading LspSettings::for_worktree → extension binary.path return → ExtensionLspAdapter LanguageServerBinary → lsp Command::new.

findings.title: Zip Slip in extension download_file extraction writes outside the extension work directory
findings.description: WASI extensions call host `download_file` with `DownloadedFileType::Zip`. The destination directory is confined with `writeable_path_from_extension`, but `node_runtime::extract_zip` joins each zip entry name onto that destination with no `..` / absolute-path rejection and no post-join `starts_with(destination)` check. A zip member such as `../../pwned` therefore writes outside the extension work dir. GzipTar uses async-tar which skips `..` entries; Zip does not. Malicious or compromised extension WASM (or a compromised download URL an extension fetches) can plant files anywhere the Zed user can write.
findings.impact: Arbitrary filesystem write as the Zed user from extension-controlled zip downloads, enabling persistence, config overwrite, or staging a binary later executed via LSP/formatter sinks.
findings.attack_path:
1. Malicious extension WASM (or compromised release asset URL) calls `download_file(url, rel_path, Zip)`.
2. Host resolves `rel_path` under the extension work dir (allowed).
3. Zip contains `../../.config/zed/...` or similar traversal members.
4. `extract_zip` writes those members outside the work dir.
5. Attacker later triggers execution of planted content or overwrites trusted config.
findings.remediation: After joining each zip entry to the destination, reject absolute paths and ensure `normalize_path(joined).starts_with(canonicalize(destination))`. Apply the same checks used by async-tar's `unpack_in`. Add regression tests for `../` and absolute entry names.
findings.poc_video_notes: Zip Slip write escaped a temp destination in a local Python reproduction of the join-without-check algorithm (`../../pwned.txt` written beside the intended extract root).

findings.title: WASM extension sandbox does not confine language_server_command process execution
findings.description: Extension WASI contexts only preopen the extension work directory, and download/write helpers use `writeable_path_from_extension`. However `ExtensionLspAdapter::get_language_server_command` uses `path_from_extension`, which joins/normalizes without requiring the result to stay under the work dir. Absolute command paths replace the prefix (`work_dir.join("/bin/sh")` → `/bin/sh`), and the host then spawns that binary with extension-supplied args/env. Extension packages are fetched over HTTPS from the Zed API with no cryptographic signature or checksum verification (checksum file is only a TODO). A malicious marketplace extension therefore gets full host code execution despite the WASI FS sandbox.
findings.impact: Installing or auto-updating a malicious/compromised extension yields immediate host RCE. The WASI sandbox does not contain process creation.
findings.attack_path:
1. Attacker publishes or compromises an extension that returns `Command { command: "/bin/sh", args: ["-c", "…"] }` from `language_server_command` (or returns a relative `../` path that normalizes outside the work dir).
2. User installs/updates the extension; archive is unpacked with no signature check.
3. User opens a file that starts the extension language server.
4. Host spawns the returned absolute path → attacker code runs.
findings.remediation: Cryptographically verify extension payloads. Treat `language_server_command` results that escape the extension work dir as requiring explicit user approval, or restrict spawn to binaries previously downloaded into the work dir / `which` allowlist. Document that extensions are fully trusted code.
findings.poc_video_notes: Validated by code audit of path_from_extension vs writeable_path_from_extension and the LSP spawn path; no malicious extension was installed in this environment.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /telemetry/crashes uploads PublicRead crash objects and can ping Slack
findings.description: In API mode, `events::router` is mounted without `validate_api_token`. `POST /telemetry/crashes` accepts an IPS body with no checksum or auth, uploads it to the `zed-crash-reports` bucket with `ObjectCannedAcl::PublicRead`, and, when configured, POSTs a Slack webhook including a public URL to the object. Hang uploads under `/telemetry/hangs` also use PublicRead (hangs require checksum; crashes do not).
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the collab API can store arbitrary content as a publicly readable S3 object under attacker-influenced keys and spam the panics Slack channel with forged crash notifications.
findings.attack_path:
1. Attacker sends POST `/telemetry/crashes` with a syntactically valid IPS report for a non-dev bundle_id and version ≥ 0.123.0.
2. Server puts the body to S3 with PublicRead ACL.
3. Optional Slack webhook fires with a link to the public object.
4. Attacker fetches the public URL or repeats to flood Slack/S3.
findings.remediation: Require the same checksum (or stronger auth) used by `/telemetry/hangs` and `/telemetry/events`. Store crash objects as private and serve via short-lived signed URLs. Rate-limit and size-cap unauthenticated telemetry.
findings.poc_video_notes: Validated by route/auth audit; no live S3/Slack call made.

findings.title: Auto-update and remote-server downloads install payloads without signature or hash verification
findings.description: Latest release metadata is fetched from the Zed HTTP API and deserialized into `{ version, url }`. The client GETs `release.url` with redirect following enabled and writes the body to disk, then extracts/installs (Linux `tar -xzf`, macOS DMG attach/copy). There is no signature, checksum, or certificate pinning check on the downloaded editor or `zed-remote-server` binary. Extension installs similarly trust HTTPS bytes with only an optional Content-Length match.
findings.impact: Compromise of the release API, CDN, or a redirect target can deliver a trojaned Zed or remote-server binary that replaces the installed app, yielding persistent host RCE for all auto-update users.
findings.attack_path:
1. Attacker compromises api.zed.dev release metadata or a hop on `release.url` (redirects allowed).
2. Client downloads attacker bytes to a temp path.
3. `install_release_linux` / macOS installer replaces the running app bits.
4. Next launch executes attacker code.
findings.remediation: Publish ed25519/minisign (or platform code-signing) signatures beside releases; verify before extract/install. Pin expected hashes in the API response and refuse redirects to unexpected hosts. Mirror the same checks for remote-server and extension downloads.
findings.poc_video_notes: No live compromise simulated. Absence of verify/signature/checksum use confirmed by full-file search of auto_update and extension install paths.

findings.title: StopCancellation billing path does not bind subscription_id to the authenticated customer
findings.description: Billing routes sit behind the shared collab `API_TOKEN` BFF. `manage_billing_subscription` loads the user from client-supplied `github_user_id` and loads `subscription_id` independently. For `StopCancellation`, it updates that Stripe subscription without checking `subscription.billing_customer_id == customer.id`. A caller that holds the API token (or a buggy BFF that forwards client IDs) can clear `cancel_at_period_end` on another user's subscription.
findings.impact: Cross-customer subscription cancellation-stop (IDOR) whenever the API token holder trusts client-provided `subscription_id` / `github_user_id` pairs.
findings.attack_path:
1. Obtain a valid collab API token (BFF or leaked `API_TOKEN`).
2. POST `/billing/subscriptions/manage` with victim `subscription_id`, attacker or victim `github_user_id`, and intent `stop_cancellation`.
3. Handler updates Stripe subscription without ownership check.
findings.remediation: Before Stripe updates, assert the subscription's `billing_customer_id` matches the customer row for the authenticated user. Prefer deriving the user from the BFF session rather than trusting body `github_user_id`.
findings.poc_video_notes: Validated by code audit of StopCancellation branch; no Stripe calls made.

findings.title: Collab service secrets committed in-repo (.env.toml and postgrest_app.conf)
findings.description: The collab crate ships `.env.toml` and `postgrest_app.conf` containing non-placeholder credentials and connection material (blob-store access key/secret, checksum seed, database URLs, PostgREST JWT secret, LLM API secret, etc.). `env.rs` loads `.env.toml` into process environment for local runs. Values are not repeated here.
findings.impact: Anyone with repo access can reuse committed credentials against whatever environments those values still protect, or use them as a template to find similarly named secrets in deployments.
findings.attack_path:
1. Clone the repository.
2. Read `crates/collab/.env.toml` and `crates/collab/postgrest_app.conf`.
3. Attempt reuse of listed credentials against reachable blob store / DB / JWT consumers.
findings.remediation: Remove secrets from git history, rotate all exposed credentials, and replace committed files with `.env.toml.example` / conf examples containing placeholders only. Load secrets from a secret manager or local untracked env files.
findings.poc_video_notes: Confirmed key presence and non-placeholder lengths without exporting secret values.
